title: A promising outlook: the top priorities for chief sustainability officers today
gist: The WEF's inaugural Chief Sustainability Officers' Outlook (103 CSOs) finds nearly two-thirds expect global sustainability progress to hold or accelerate, with a stronger business case (64%) and cheaper sustainable tech (56%) as top accelerators, while geopolitics, policy uncertainty and inflation make execution uneven. CSOs from ADNOC, Zurich Insurance, Standard Chartered and Mastercard describe the shift from targets to capital allocation: 'pathway realism' on energy transition, climate adaptation rising fast (80%+ expect more focus), insurability-driven resilience spending, and circular consumption (second-hand clothing +28% vs +8% for clothing stores in 2025).

themes.theme: CSO Outlook survey: momentum holds, drivers shift

insights.claim: In the World Economic Forum's inaugural Chief Sustainability Officers' Outlook survey of 103 CSOs, nearly two-thirds expect global sustainability progress to hold steady or accelerate over the next year despite geopolitical tensions and short-term business pressures.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Corporate sustainability budgets look sticky rather than collapsing under political backlash — supports continued (if slower) demand for transition and ESG-adjacent services.

insights.claim: Surveyed CSOs name a stronger business case (64%) and lower-cost, more widely available sustainable technologies (56%) as the leading accelerators of sustainability progress over the next three years — i.e. economics, not regulation, is now seen as the primary driver.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Transition exposure should be underwritten on cost-curve and ROI grounds, not policy support; favor technologies already at or near cost parity.

insights.claim: The CSO agenda is shifting from ambition to execution, with sustainability increasingly embedded in planning, investment and operations rather than confined to commitments, targets and reporting, while geopolitical volatility and policy uncertainty make progress uneven.
insights.speaker: Marisa Drew
insights.so_what: Watch capex allocation and asset-level decisions rather than target announcements as the real signal of corporate transition commitment.

insights.claim: Standard Chartered's CSO argues that policy uncertainty, geopolitics and inflation raising near-term execution pressure may ultimately strengthen sustainability by forcing it to evolve from a commitment into a capability enabler for growth, competitiveness and resilience.
insights.speaker: Marisa Drew
insights.so_what: The backlash period may weed out commitment-only programs and concentrate spend in value-accretive projects — favor companies whose green capex has standalone returns.
insights.quote: But this pressure may ultimately make sustainability stronger

insights.claim: CSOs overwhelmingly expect AI and other digital technologies to aid sustainability progress, while acknowledging trade-offs from AI's own environmental and social impacts.
insights.speaker: Marisa Drew
insights.so_what: AI's energy/resource footprint is recognized inside corporates but not treated as a reason to slow adoption — corporate climate targets will bend around AI demand.

insights.claim: ADNOC's sustainability chief argues there is no single energy transition and no single speed: energy systems will decarbonize through different technology and capital combinations shaped by each market's energy mix, and uneven, non-linear progress reflects economics rather than wavering ambition.
insights.speaker: Ibrahim Al-Zu'bi
insights.so_what: National oil companies are publicly framing a multi-speed transition that legitimizes sustained hydrocarbon investment — supportive of long-duration upstream capex assumptions.
insights.quote: There is no single transition and no single speed.

insights.claim: ADNOC positions energy security as more critical than ever and argues it is met by producers able to deliver through uncertainty, built on long-term investment, disciplined operations and durable partnerships.
insights.speaker: Ibrahim Al-Zu'bi
insights.so_what: Energy-security framing elevates reliable Gulf producers' strategic value in a volatile geopolitical environment.
insights.quote: Energy security is more critical today than ever

insights.claim: ADNOC assesses physical and transition climate risk asset by asset under recognized climate and economic scenarios and feeds the results into asset integrity planning and capital decisions, placing carbon management inside business planning rather than alongside it.
insights.speaker: Ibrahim Al-Zu'bi
insights.so_what: Asset-level climate-risk integration into capex is becoming the standard for large energy producers; laggards face higher cost of capital and insurance.
insights.locator: Ibrahim Al-Zu'bi, ADNOC: out of compliance thinking

insights.claim: ADNOC frames sustainability as bigger than emissions ('sustainability with a big S'), extending to resource management, community support and education as rising energy demand places more responsibility on producers.
insights.speaker: Ibrahim Al-Zu'bi
insights.so_what: Producers are broadening the definition of sustainability away from emissions metrics — expect ESG narratives from oil majors to emphasize social license over decarbonization pace.
insights.quote: We call our approach sustainability with a big S
insights.locator: Ibrahim Al-Zu'bi, ADNOC: bigger than emissions

themes.theme: Adaptation and insurability as a business case

insights.claim: Over 80% of surveyed CSOs expect greater global focus on climate adaptation in the year ahead, and over 75% believe private-sector investment will help adaptation scale.
insights.speaker: Marisa Drew
insights.so_what: Adaptation (resilient infrastructure, risk engineering, flood/heat protection) is the fastest-rising corporate climate spend category — a growth theme distinct from mitigation.

insights.claim: Zurich Insurance treats climate risk as a business risk affecting continuity, operations, supply chains, investment decisions and the availability and affordability of insurance, and manages adaptation through its Climate Transition Plan.
insights.speaker: Linda Freiner
insights.so_what: Insurance availability/affordability is the transmission channel that turns physical climate risk into corporate P&L and asset-value risk — monitor premium repricing in exposed regions.

insights.claim: Adaptation investments often lack an immediate or easily measured return because their value lies in avoided losses, business continuity and faster recovery; insurers' climate data, modelling and risk engineering can quantify that value to make the case for prevention.
insights.speaker: Linda Freiner
insights.so_what: Insurers are positioning risk engineering and climate analytics as a revenue/advisory line and a lever to keep risks insurable — an under-appreciated growth vector for large P&C carriers.
insights.quote: By bringing clearer risk insight to business decisions, we can help customers make a stronger case for adaptation.

insights.claim: Zurich says continued insurability for customers depends partly on working with governments on resilient infrastructure and effective public policy for adaptation.
insights.speaker: Linda Freiner
insights.so_what: Implicit warning that without public adaptation spending some risks become uninsurable — relevant for real estate and municipal credit in high-hazard areas.

themes.theme: Circular consumption and sustainable spending data

insights.claim: Mastercard Economics Institute's report 'The Next Era of Conscious Consumption' found that in the top 20 circular shopping economies, second-hand clothing sales grew 28% year over year in 2025 versus 8% growth at clothing stores.
insights.speaker: Ellen Jackowski
insights.so_what: Resale is taking share from primary apparel retail at a ~3.5x growth differential — positive for resale platforms, a structural headwind for fast-fashion volumes.
insights.quote: second-hand clothing sales increased 28% year over year in 2025, compared to 8% growth in clothing stores

insights.claim: Mastercard uses payments data to track where second-hand, reuse and rental models are gaining traction and how behaviour varies across generations and markets, and argues CSOs should capitalize on shifts toward sustainable spending to create new business value.
insights.speaker: Ellen Jackowski
insights.so_what: Card-spend data is an early indicator of circular-economy adoption; watch payment-network research for leading reads on resale/rental category growth.
